t: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen
s: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen -- GROWTH CHAMBER · PRE-PIVOT · WEEK Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen Our first plan was a sealed growth chamber with hydroponics inside it. Arabidopsis needs steady humidity, temperature and light to give comparable results, and the school lab could not hold any of those steady. The chamber was meant to give us a controlled box to run every plant experiment in. This was the last week of design before we started buying parts. t: Visiting Prof. Verslues
s: Visiting Prof. Verslues HB HUMIDITY BOX · ORIGIN · CONSULTATION Visiting Prof. Verslues We had a chamber design nobody had agreed to and a purchasing freeze. None of us had seen a working plant growth setup, so we went to look at one before designing any more of our own. Incubator shelf with vertical agar plates Photometer we saw at his lab that measures cell density DECISION Build a humidity box, not a growth chamber Small enough that we’d actually finish it. Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up. REJECTED Carrying on with the full chamber. It was frozen anyway, and after seeing a real one we couldn’t justify the size. PROBLEMS HOW WE’LL FIX IT No target humidity range written down, and nothing to measure it with SINCE THIS WEEK → Get the range Arabidopsis needs, and put a sensor on the next electronics order. NEXT Design the box around a target humidity range, not around the space we happen to have. PROJECT Humidity box · origin DATE 05/04/2026 ENTRY 2 pre Visited Prof. Verslues’s lab at Academia Sinica on 3 April. Looked at how his incubator holds conditions across a whole tray at once. – Trays sit on wire shelving with airflow coming from underneath. – He grows at a much lower density than we had been planning for. – Came back and dropped the full chamber in favour of a humidity box. t: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start
s: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start BR BIOREACTOR · CONCEPT · CONSULTATION The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start This is the week the project changed shape. t: Dropping the fluorometer
s: Dropping the fluorometer FL/PH FLUOROMETER · PHOTOMETER · WEEK Dropping the fluorometer The chlorophyll fluorometer would have let us measure plant stress directly, by reading damage to photosystem II. Fv/Fm is the standard number for that, and a healthy plant sits around 0.78 to 0.83. It was the fourth instrument we had in progress and there were three of us. The Open-JIP layout we evaluated (published figure, shared in #dry-fluorometer on 9 April) 13 May: checking agar plants by eye, the measurement a fluorometer would have replaced pre Made the case for building it. t: Humidity box finished, agar photos useless
s: Humidity box finished, agar photos useless HB HUMIDITY BOX · IMAGING STATION · BUILD Humidity box finished, agar photos useless The humidity box is a small sealed enclosure that keeps humidity steady while Arabidopsis germinates. It came out of the Verslues visit and it is the first thing we finished. The same week we started growing on agar plates, and ran into a problem we had not planned for. 21 May: the electronics run at Guanghua market DECISION Build a station instead of writing a procedure A written procedure still depends on whoever is holding the phone. If the geometry is locked in plastic, the photos come out comparable whether you’re careful or not. REJECTED A tripod and a taped mark on the bench. Cheaper, does nothing about room light, and it’s wrong the moment someone moves the tripod. HB-1 Finished the humidity box and put the first seeds in. We have no log of what humidity and temperature it actually holds. – Started photographing agar plates to track germination. The photos were useless. The angle moved between shots, the room light changed with the time of day, and the shadows moved with it. – Two plates photographed on different days told us nothing about how much had grown. – Spent two afternoons shooting a transparent dish on a white table, trying to find a repeatable setup by hand. It did not work, but it told us what was moving: angle, distance, background

t: Bioreactor prototype I built
s: Bioreactor prototype I built BR BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · BUILD Bioreactor prototype I built The bioreactor is the vessel the pivot committed us to. Bacteria live inside a hollow fibre membrane while the protectant they make crosses the membrane and leaves, which keeps the organism contained. Prototype I is the simplest version of that we could build. 6 June: prototype I on the bench, culture going in Prototype I as designed: membrane, pump, sampling valve, reservoir BR-1 Built prototype I on 6 June from four parts. PES hollow fibre membrane with around 200 mL of lumen volume, a 500 mL reservoir holding 300 mL of LB, a peristaltic pump, and a luer valve on the loop for sampling. – Inoculated with 20 mL of a multi-overnight B. subtilis culture. Deliberately left everything else off. No stirring, no aeration, no pH control. We did not know which of those we needed. Starting with none means every addition later has a reason behind it we can point at. – Adding them all at once would have meant several things failing together with no way to tell which mattered. – Drove both light plate wavelengths for the first time, green 520 nm and red 660 nm. First row of wells only, driven independently. Green is the on command for the CcaS-CcaR circuit and red is the off command. – WEEK 14 1 – 7 JUNE 2026 19 1 June: light plate, first light in both colours TABLE 9 Component Spec Note Membrane

t: The cells barely grow in the reactor
s: The cells barely grow in the reactor BR BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · FAILURE DIAGNOSIS The cells barely grow in the reactor This is the first run of prototype I. We grew the same culture in the reactor and in a flask at the same time, both at room temperature, so the flask acts as a control. If the reactor works, the two curves should look alike. SYMPTOM Paired growth curves against a flask control at room temperature. The flask climbed past 2.4 over 25 hours. The reactor stayed almost flat and ended near 0.3, and the run terminated early on a leak at the pump. Prototype I loop on the bench: pump, membrane cartridge, reservoir OD600 against time: flask (blue) to ~2.4, reactor (orange) flat near 0.3 BR-1 Sampled both arms every thirty minutes for eight hours, then again at 25 hours. One person had to stay with it for the whole run. – Got a flask that climbed past 2.4 and a reactor that stayed almost flat near 0.3. The numbers inside the system disagreed too, 0.304 in the tube against 0.48 in the reservoir. That should not happen if the loop is mixed. – Terminated early when medium leaked at the peristaltic pump. The leak was at the pump head, where the tubing flexes most. – Plated 2 mL from the shell side of the membrane on LB and got no colonies at all. That is our evidence the membrane holds the bacteria in. It came out of the run that otherwise failed. – WEEK 15 8 – 14 JUNE 202

t: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours
s: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours BR BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE II · TEST Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours Prototype I barely grew and we had four candidate reasons. Prototype II changes three of them at once, which is not how you isolate a cause, but we had weeks, not months. 14 June: sampling the reactor arm Sampling the flask arm Prototype II: stirrer under the reservoir, sampler beside it The sampling procedure, written out by hand for whoever took the next shift Page 2 of the procedure OD600 against minutes at 37 °C: reactor (orange) and flask (blue) TABLE 11 Arm Plateau OD600 Time to plateau Against prototype I Bioreactor 0.8 – 0.9 2 h flat at ~0.3 Flask control 0.6 – 0.8 4.5 h reached 2.4 at 25 h Full growth curve secured. The reactor reached plateau faster and higher than the flask. BR-2 Added a 200 rpm magnetic stirrer to the reservoir to stop cells settling out. The stirrer bar was the largest one we had, which may be part of why it worked so well. – Moved the sampling port to the reservoir outlet, where there is far more volume. A sample from there represents the whole system, not one length of tube. – Ran both arms at 37 °C instead of room temperature, pump held at 94 mL/min. Got a full growth curve, and the reactor beat its own flask control. Reactor plateaued at OD600 0.8 to 0.9 after two hours. Flask reached 0.6 to 0.8 after four and a half. – WEEK 1

t: Wrong unit for the light dose
s: Wrong unit for the light dose LP LIGHT PLATE · DOSE UNITS · TEST Wrong unit for the light dose The CcaS-CcaR circuit responds to a specific photon flux, so the light dose the plate delivers has to be a known quantity. This week we found we had been about to measure it in entirely the wrong unit. TABLE 12a Quantity Value Unit Source CcaS–CcaR half-maximal 4.66 ± 0.63 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ Castillo-Hair 2019 Hill coefficient 1.88 ± 0.16 — same t½ ON / OFF 105.1 / 74.97 min same What our meter reads — lux — units Checked the Castillo-Hair paper and found its half-maximal point is 4.66 µmol per square metre per second. That is a photon flux density. It counts photons. – Checked what our meters read, and found every affordable one reads illuminance in lux. Lux is weighted for human vision, which peaks around 555 nm. Our green sits at 520 and our red at 660, both well off that peak. – So the conversion error is not even the same size on the two channels. – Bought a lux meter and set out to derive the conversion for our own LED spectra. A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget. A phone app was considered and rejected as not repeatable between handsets. – Caught it before any dose figure went out, so nothing published needs correcting. – WEEK 16 15 – 21 JUNE 2026 No conversion factor exists; every light dose is in lux. The two units measure different things and cannot be converted without knowing

t: Temperature sensor driving the green channel
s: Temperature sensor driving the green channel LP STRESS TO LIGHT · FIRMWARE · BUILD Temperature sensor driving the green channel The whole project is one sentence: sense stress, emit light, release protectant. This is the first time the sensing end and the light end ran together on a bench, two months after the pivot. demo Wired an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor to the Arduino over I2C. It reports humidity too, which the code reads and then ignores. – Wrote a linear stress fraction between a floor and a ceiling temperature. Below 32 °C the LED is off. At 50 °C and above it is at full brightness. Between those it scales linearly. – Mapped the fraction onto a PWM green channel and ran it. The transfer function is four lines of code, deliberately. Anything more shaped would be invented, since we have no data on how stress response scales with temperature. – WEEK 16 15 – 21 JUNE 2026 TABLE 12b Constant Value Meaning TEMP_BASE 32.0 °C below this the LED is off TEMP_MAX 50.0 °C at or above this, full brightness Between linear stress fraction 0 to 1 drives PWM duty Sensor SHT31 temperature and humidity, I2C Four constants and a straight line between two of them. Wrote it up as Stress_to_Light_Demo_Manual.docx. 32 °C and 50 °C are guesses, not measurements. Only the green channel is driven, so the demo switches the circuit on but not off. – DECISION Linear between two thresholds,

t: Making the plate float
s: Making the plate float FP HYDROPONICS · FLOATING PLATE · BUILD Making the plate float Arabidopsis grows hydroponically on a plate sitting over liquid medium. The roots have to reach the liquid without the plate flooding, and our first version was fixed in place, which meant setting the level by hand every day and getting it wrong. 13 June: the fixed-plate hydroponic box in use 25 June: first floating plate, washer poles at the corners FP-1 Built a fixed plate with a liquid chamber underneath, and found the level impossible to hold. It has to sit as high as possible without coming over the growing platform, and it drops as the plants drink, so the roots end up in air. – Redesigned it to float on the medium instead. The frame of the platform is built as sealed air chambers, so it rides on the surface and stays at the same height above the liquid whatever the level does. – Calculated the buoyancy before printing, not by tuning it afterwards. A hollow frame cannot be adjusted once printed, so print orientation and wall thickness now decide whether it floats. – Added poles at the corners to take washers as weights. Adding weight is easier than adding volume, so the poles are the margin for error. The washers we have are heavier than the calculation wanted, so the adjustment is coarse. – Printed the first iteration on 25 June. chamber volume was tuned. – WEEK 17 22 – 28 JUNE 2026 A l

t: Transmembrane pressure on a screen
s: Transmembrane pressure on a screen BR BIOREACTOR · PRESSURE · BUILD Transmembrane pressure on a screen A hollow fibre membrane fouls as it runs, and fouling shows up as pressure building across the membrane. Until this week we had no way of seeing that happen, so we could not tell a clean run from a blocked one. 10 July: transducer and Luer line before fitting 12 July: transmembrane pressure live on the laptop for the first time Chars #dry-bioreactor · 12 July We can monitor the transmembrane pressure now. All we need is pinch valve and B. subtilis. DECISION Instrument the loop before fitting the valve Put a valve on a loop we can’t measure and we won’t see what it does. Pressure is what the valve is there to control. REJECTED Fitting the pinch valve first, which was already designed and waiting. Ordering it that way would have made the valve’s effect invisible. PROBLEMS HOW WE’LL FIX IT No pinch valve yet, so pressure cannot be controlled SINCE THIS WEEK → Print the valve and fit it after the membrane. Sawtooth amplitude never quantified SINCE THIS WEEK → Measure it peak to peak and check against the pump head rate. pressure Fitted a BP8G-AGA pressure transducer on the retentate side. t: LPA V3 finished
s: LPA V3 finished LP LIGHT PLATE · LPA V3 · BUILD LPA V3 finished Prototype 1 of the light plate lit one row back on 1 June. Milestone 2 asked for tunable intensity in both colours across the whole array.
